name: Qigong

card.summary: A Chinese system of slow movement, posture, breathing and meditation that practitioners use for low-impact conditioning, relaxation and sleep, which can feed into steadier training, posture and skin-and-body upkeep.
card.aka: Chi kung, Baduanjin (Eight Pieces of Brocade) as a common form
card.note: Generally described as gentle exercise; as with any movement practice, strains are possible and people with medical conditions are usually advised to check with a clinician.

quick.overview:
Qigong is a family of Chinese exercises that combine slow, flowing or held postures with deliberate breathing and focused attention. Practitioners describe it as a way to cultivate and balance qi, a traditional concept of life energy. In a looks context it is used as gentle conditioning: regular practice is associated with better posture awareness, flexibility, lower stress and better sleep, all of which people link to how they carry and present themselves.

Research consists mostly of randomised trials and reviews in older adults, cancer survivors, menopausal women and students, measuring outcomes such as sleep, mood, fatigue, frailty and muscle function. Trials on appearance itself are not part of this literature. The traditional energy explanation is a cultural framework that has not been measured directly by researchers.
quick.how: Most people learn a set routine, often Baduanjin (Eight Pieces of Brocade), from a class, book or video. Sessions are typically 15 to 30 minutes of slow standing movements, sometimes with static stance holding (zhan zhuang) or seated breathing. It is commonly done daily or several times a week and used alongside strength training or other exercise as a recovery or warm-up practice.
quick.risks: Qigong is generally regarded as low-risk physical activity, with the usual risks of muscle strain from deep stances. Chinese sources historically describe a condition called qigong deviation, a psychological disturbance reported after intensive practice in the 1980s and 1990s. Claims that qigong can replace medical treatment are not supported by clinical guidelines, which list it as a complementary option for symptoms such as fatigue.

lead: Qigong is a Chinese mind-body practice that combines coordinated posture and movement, breathing and meditation. Practitioners say it cultivates and balances qi, a traditional notion of life force, and use it for recreation, relaxation, preventive health and martial training [1][2].

For people interested in improving how they look, qigong sits on the recovery and body-care side of the ledger. Slow, low-impact forms such as Baduanjin involve horse stances, spinal and neck stretches and balance work, which practitioners describe as supporting posture, mobility, stress reduction and sleep. Better sleep and lower stress are themselves things many people connect with skin, energy and physique [3][4].

Research on qigong consists mostly of randomised trials and reviews examining mood, sleep, fatigue, frailty, bone density and physical function in specific groups. A cancer-fatigue guideline from ASCO and the Society for Integrative Oncology lists tai chi or qigong among recommended options during treatment [5]. No published trial has measured facial or physique appearance as an outcome.

chain: Slow stance, stretch and breathing sequences
Easier training, upright carriage, calmer presentation
angle.text: People use qigong as a daily low-intensity routine alongside lifting or sport, as mobility work and a way to wind down. Practitioners link the resulting posture, flexibility and sleep to a more upright, relaxed look.

infobox: China; modern term coined in the 1940s-50s [1]
Public practice limited to state-approved forms since 1999-2000 [1]

paras: Qigong (also spelled chi kung) is classified by writers into dynamic forms with flowing movement, static forms that hold postures, meditative forms centred on breath awareness and visualisation, and forms involving external aids such as massage or a teacher said to transmit qi [1]. Tai chi and some martial arts are treated by many sources as related or overlapping practices [1].

Baduanjin, the Eight Pieces of Brocade, is one of the most widely practised health forms. Its standing set includes movements such as holding the hands up to the sky, drawing a bow in a low stance, turning the head to look backward, swaying the head and tail in a squat, reaching down to hold the feet, clenching the fists with a fierce gaze, and rising on the toes [2]. It is classed as medical qigong and is also used by martial artists as supplementary exercise [2].

Chinese guided-breathing and stretching exercises (daoyin) appear in a painting from a Western Han tomb of the second century BC, and qigong's roots are traced to medicine, Daoism, Buddhism, Confucianism and martial arts [1]. The word qigong as the name of a health practice is credited to Liu Guizhen around 1949, and his 1957 book was an early publication on the subject [1].

Baduanjin appears in Song-dynasty texts, with a form illustrated around 1300 in Ten Compilations on Cultivating Perfection, which credits two of the Eight Immortals with its creation. Later sources attributed it to the general Yue Fei, a link historian Meir Shahar traces to a 1624 preface [2].

Qigong was criticised and banned in the mid-1960s, rehabilitated from 1979, recognised as a standard medical technique in 1989, and reached an estimated 60 to 200 million practitioners in the 1990s [1]. In 1999 authorities closed clinics and banned groups including Falun Gong and Zhong Gong, and in 2000 the Chinese Health Qigong Association was founded to regulate approved forms and instructors [1].

Practitioners describe qi circulating through meridians and say practice balances it for health and longevity [1][6]. Martial claims such as Iron Shirt and Iron Palm, in which training is said to let the body withstand strikes, are also attributed to qigong training [1]. Proponents emphasise that it is low-impact and accessible to older people, people with disabilities and those recovering from injury [1].
Scientific reviewers have noted that investigations of paranormal qigong claims in 1980s China did not produce replicable results [1].

Qigong trials usually measure health outcomes rather than appearance. A systematic review and meta-analysis of mind-body exercise, including qigong and baduanjin, in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women examined bone mineral density, sleep, anxiety, depression and fatigue [7]. A randomised trial of a qigong programme in Spanish postmenopausal women examined sleep quality, anxiety and depression [8]. A 24-week randomised trial tested Baduanjin for sarcopenia, age-related loss of muscle, in older adults [9], and randomised trials have tested qigong for frailty in older cancer survivors [10][11].

A 2023 randomised trial examined Baduanjin on the physical and mental health of college students [12]. A meta-analysis of randomised trials of Baduanjin looked at health benefits across several outcomes [13], and a 2010 review examined both qigong and tai chi trials [14].

The 2024 ASCO and Society for Integrative Oncology guideline on cancer-related fatigue found, in its review of 113 trials, that tai chi, qigong and American ginseng showed benefit during treatment and recommended that clinicians suggest tai chi or qigong to reduce fatigue; it rated certainty of evidence for these interventions as low to moderate [5]. Qigong also appears among the exercise types compared in a network meta-analysis for pain in women with fibromyalgia [15].

Reviews summarised on Wikipedia describe methodological limits in this field, including small samples, weak controls and difficulty blinding participants; a 2026 umbrella review reportedly found high-certainty evidence for traditional Chinese exercises in areas such as knee osteoarthritis pain and fibromyalgia sleep [1].

Qigong is generally regarded as safe, with risks similar to other gentle physical activity such as muscle strains or sprains, and clinical sources advise consulting a physician when combining it with conventional treatment [1]. In China, the 1980s and 1990s boom was accompanied by reports of qigong deviation, a mental condition attributed to intensive or unsupervised practice, and of cult-like groups, which contributed to later regulation [1].

lore.intro: Qigong is discussed mainly as a general wellness and mobility practice rather than as an appearance protocol.

claims.claim: Qigong cultivates and balances qi for health and vitality
claims.believers: Practitioners describe qi flowing through meridians and say regular practice restores balance and energy [1].
claims.experts: Researchers have studied qigong's measurable effects on sleep, mood, fatigue and function rather than qi itself; trials do not measure qi directly [5][8].

claims.claim: Slow qigong routines improve sleep, mood and fatigue
claims.believers: Practitioners report feeling calmer and more rested after sessions [1].
claims.experts: Randomised trials and guidelines have examined these outcomes in groups such as postmenopausal women and cancer patients, with the ASCO guideline rating certainty as low to moderate [5][8].

claims.claim: Baduanjin builds strength and slows muscle loss
claims.believers: Proponents say its stances and movements work the waist, legs and arms and suit older people [2].
claims.experts: A 24-week randomised trial has tested Baduanjin for sarcopenia in older adults [9].

claims.claim: Qigong training can make the body withstand blows (Iron Shirt, Iron Palm)
claims.believers: Martial lineages attribute such feats to specialised qigong training [1].
claims.experts: The Wikipedia summary notes these claims are not backed by strong evidence [1].
